en: And destroy you, Jediger,
If I do not scatter your myriad herds,
Leaving you nothing at all,
And wipe out your people utterly,
Then rage as you will, hero Kyyaz!
If I do not raid your six valleys,
And thus devise your ruin,
If I do not massacre
All your boastful people,
Bring the death of vengeance upon you,
And turn your honor into ashes,
Setting right your arrogance
And stripping you of power,
If I do not slaughter multitudes of you,
Leaving not one hair’s breadth of a man,
And destroy you, Jediger—
With his keen, Zulfiqar-like sword,
Does Kanchoro, who fears no bloodshed,
Fear to drive out
You, the massed black Jediger?
This slave fears no hero;
Do you think
Your warrior fears to lay you low?
Know well what I have said;
My hero Kyyaz, heed my words.
Jylgyn, Keng-Kol, and broad Talas
Are no lands where we can linger at ease.
What do you say, Kyyaz, alas,
Of Külchoro, Almambet’s son?
He is more than a match for both of us.
If by chance we leave him untouched,
If by chance we do not assail him,
He will recover from his sickness
And turn again toward battle;
He will recover from his wounds
And return firmly to the fray.
If we leave that warrior to himself,
His aching wounds will heal.
A wounded man who spares his foe
Will see Kyyaz’s blood spilled.
If we do not assail Külchoro,
Will his day of triumph not dawn?
Will he not pursue us as far as Köykap?
If that warrior is enraged,
Will he not make a spectacle of slaughter?
Will he not leave not one of you
And massacre you all?
Will he not utterly plunder
The Jediger’s women and girls?
When Külchoro meets an army,
He grinds it down like sand and flour.
He makes them drink his furious venom,
Surrounds, slaughters, and batters them,
And finishes them within two days.
He will raise red slaughter and turmoil,
And bring great misery and uproar.
He will empty the bullets from his cartridge pouch;
When his wild fury seizes him,
He will wipe out many of you.
You are a lord, hero Kyyaz—
Will he not trample over our heads?
Will he not crush the lords,
Dig a well in the place of honor,
Ransack all your bundles,
And scatter your four kinds of livestock?
Will he not dig a well in the place of honor,
Turn upon us and wreak havoc,
And avenge every ancient grudge?
Once that warrior has recovered,
Will he not rip your belly open like a donkey’s?
Foolish Kyyaz, may ruin take you!
Should the two of us be left alone,
Will he not dig your road to doom,
Bind your hands behind your back,
Strip off your coat as booty,
Break through your gorge and make a road,
And disgrace your bloodied head?
Good fortune to you, hero Kyyaz—
Will he not seize you by the scruff?
Will he not bind us together
And exhibit us to the Dångyt?
Will he not cut off your head like a sheep’s?
If you fall into Külchoro’s hands,
Will he not split your belly like a melon?
He has ground the rugged mountains into grease—
Külchoro, whose father was Chinese,
Who laid his own elder brother low,
Who never shrank from a face-to-face fight
And never turned back from shedding blood.
Such is the warrior’s nature.
He drinks and is never sated with blood;
The man who fights him is left crawling.
He never retreats from combat,
And when he charges in fury,
He never turns back before drinking blood.
How can you make that black-hearted warrior
Your kinsman?
By counting an enemy as kin,
Now and at every turn,
You have proved a witless Kyyaz,
One who never dares a great risk,
Who cannot step outdoors at night—
You are a coward, Kyyaz,
Without a shred of sense;
A cowardly Kyyaz indeed.
You are a Kyyaz who brings
Disaster upon his own life,
A Kyyaz who will ravage
And destroy his own people,
A Kyyaz who will drive an arrow
Into his own body,
A Kyyaz who will surrender
His own life to death.
If you mean to deliver him as bloody spoil to the slaughterer,
Speak the truth;
If you mean to take the formidable woman Aichürök,
Speak the truth about that as well.”
The utterly wicked Kanchoro
Made his cruel wrath known,
And forced the massed black Jediger
To join our side.
They hailed the Jediger’s hero Kyyaz
As comrade and champion,
And swore, “Let any man who disobeys
Have an infidel for a father!”
They took a death-bound oath
And swiftly made their pledge.
The massed black Jediger
All raised an uproar,
And took the black-hearted Kanchoro
As their commander.
They raised a moon-crested banner
And gathered an army whose roar split the sky,
Not a small host, but a multitude.
They chose the finest from among thousands,
Men skilled and ready with the spear,
To search together and find
The wounded, suffering hero
Külchoro,
To cast him into a dungeon forty ropes deep
If he fell into their hands,
And take his head with the sword.
Nursing his hatred, Kanchoro set out
To find Külchoro,
Gouge out both his eyes,
And, without sparing his fly-like soul,
Flay him while he screamed.
The pale-mottled standards thronged,
And a wailing clamor arose.
They girded on unsheathed swords
And made their weapons ready.
With shafts of steel and sharpened points,
Black tempered blades fitted to their tips,
Double-edged and four-sided,
They bore countless steel spears.
Now they searched for the warrior.
Wearing great boots with horseshoe heels,
Külchoro had crossed
The rugged hills and ridges;
Külchoro had passed beyond them.
Through Kara-Buura and Chatkal
Külchoro had ridden like the wind.
Plainly he had crossed
Kara-Üngkür of the soothsayer
And arrived there.
Once Kanchoro and Külchoro
Ate the Kyrgyz people’s yellow butter,
Ate fat young mares that had never foaled,
Rode colts and flew hunting birds,
Played shabiyet and made merry,
Laughing until the sun went down
And feasting until dawn.
When bored, they shot roe deer;
When not bored, they spent their time
Playing freely.
They had grown up together tending horses,
But alas, Kanchoro was ill-fated.
They had crossed open country and seen many peoples,
Gathered horses and seen many lands.
Out there in Kara-Buura and Chatkal,
He must have been unable to flee farther.
Kara-Üngkür of the soothsayer,
The true cave where people hid—
The warrior must have fled there
And crouched concealed within.
With hero Kyyaz in his train,
Kanchoro led the host.
They followed poor Külchoro,
Placing grass upon his fading tracks,
And pursued him until they grew pale;
They flung dust upon his fresh trail
And chased him in a frenzy.
Three times around
The pass of Üyrülmö
They pursued him without tiring.
Twilight fell and the sun went down,
And the whole host lay silent.
When they had slept their fill,
The swift steeds tugged and plunged
As they cropped the feather grass.
When dawn began to swell,
And light touched the earth,
The stars scattered from overhead,
As daybreak opened wide.
The stars vanished one by one from the sky,
And the cold wind before sunrise shivered;
The stars streamed from the heavens,
And every living creature
Rose from its place, calling out.
The willow branches bent,
Lines were traced across the sand,
The reed tops trembled,
And young larks chirped over the steppe.
The yellow dawn broke,
And Libra sank from the sky.
Mist thinned from mountain after mountain,
And countless springs poured through the ravines.
Ninety kinds of birds sang plaintively,
And the nightingale’s voice was heard;
The cuckoo called melodiously,
And all kinds of woodland birds
Began to speak.
Wild goats cried from the heights,
And stags called from the knolls.
The fog lifted everywhere,
Light spread over the earth,
And when the land came into view,
The horse beneath him
Was Köbösh Khan’s Kökborchuk.
Upon that racer Kökborchuk,
Striking right and left with his whip,
Your hero Kanchoro
Rode on in feverish haste,
The consummate, accursed villain,
Madly searching for Külchoro.
When he looked toward Kara-Üngkür,
Eager to find Külchoro,
He saw the cave mouth had been covered
And that across its entrance
Rotten grass had been scattered.
The hero Külchoro was hidden there,
But the heel mark of his horseshoe-soled boot
Stood out plainly in the open.
Kanchoro halted and shouted,
Calling to hero Kyyaz
Of the Jediger:
“Fortunate hero Kyyaz,
Your campaign has prospered!
What you lost has come onto your road;
Though delayed, your luck has turned—
Your fugitive has come onto your road.
Hero Kyyaz of the Jediger,
Your old good fortune has returned.
Let your wrestlers and lions,
Your heroes who boast of their strength,
Your able men skilled with the spear,
